title: Proficiency Grammar (Essential Grammar in Use - Murphy)
lesson_overview: C2 level near-native precision, idiomatic density, and genre-specific structures for exceptional mastery of English nuance and style.

topics.name: Near-native Precision
topics.lesson_text: Exceptionally fine distinctions in meaning and style. English has many near-synonyms with subtle differences: claim vs allege vs assert vs maintain vs suggest. Verb patterns with subtle meaning shifts: help somebody (to) do vs help do. Passive vs active voice choices for emphasis. Modal verbs with extreme certainty: must surely vs can possibly vs may well. Cleft sentences: It was the lawyer who defended him. Pseudo-cleft: What he did was leave. Note: Native-like precision requires understanding connotation, collocation, and pragmatic appropriacy, not just grammatical correctness. Advanced irony, understatement, litotes.
examples: He claimed he was innocent. vs He alleged the money was missing. vs He asserted his rights. vs He maintained his position. vs He suggested leaving early.
It was such a lovely day that we decided to picnic.
It was the chef who cooked the meal.

topics.name: Idiomatic Density
topics.lesson_text: Fixed idioms and expressions that cannot be understood literally. Hundreds of common idioms: beat around the bush, cut corners, hit the nail on the head, once in a blue moon, piece of cake, spill the beans. Collocations: words that frequently go together (make a decision, not do a decision; strong coffee, not powerful coffee). Metaphorical language: time flies, a ray of hope, the foot of the mountain. Phrasal verbs with specific meanings: give up, give in, give out. Note: Idioms are context-dependent; some are informal, some neutral, some literary. Mastery involves recognizing and using appropriate idioms for register and context.
examples: He finally admitted he was wrong. vs He finally came clean.
She's feeling under the weather today.
You really should apply yourself more.

topics.name: Rhetorical Devices
topics.lesson_text: Rhetorical devices for persuasive and literary effect. Contrast: not only...but also, whereas, while, in contrast. Emphasis: it is...that, as...as, fronting. Concession: although, even though, despite, in spite of, while. Rhetorical questions: Who could possibly disagree?. Repetition: We shall fight on the beaches. Antithesis: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times. Note: Devices depend on context and purpose; literary vs persuasive vs everyday use. Advanced connector phrases: notwithstanding, not to mention, let alone.
examples: Although it was raining, the game continued.
Not only did he win, but he also set a record.
Hardly had I arrived when the phone rang.

topics.name: Genre-specific
topics.lesson_text: Genre-specific linguistic features. Academic: passive voice frequent, impersonal structures, objective tone, hedging (may, might, can, could, appear to, seem), complex sentence structures, formal vocabulary (utilize vs use, whereas vs but). Creative: figurative language, sensory detail, Show don't tell, dialogue patterns, stream of consciousness. Business: concise communication, standard format, clear action orientation, effective email structure, report organization. Note: Genre conventions vary within broad categories; academic disciplines have specific norms; business genres (email, report, proposal) have standard structures. Register alignment with purpose and audience is crucial.
examples: Academic: The study revealed a significant correlation. Business: We are pleased to inform you that. Creative: The dawn crept over the hills, shy and golden.

cefr_description: Can understand with ease virtually everything heard or read and can summarise information from different spoken and written sources, reconstructing arguments and accounts in a coherent presentation.
